payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the image show the original visual content rendered in a pencil-drawn style?
node.criteria: Pass if the image visibly represents its content as a pencil drawing; fail if there is sufficient evidence that no pencil-drawing transformation has occurred; unknown if the image or its style cannot be assessed reliably. Partial evidence of a pencil-drawn style is progress, not completion.
node.binding: Compare the supplied image with the requested transformation: assess whether its visual content is rendered in a pencil-drawn style. Do not require a particular pencil technique.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and outlines.

The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting, but renders them with muted, mostly monochrome tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them in a muted, textured pencil-drawing style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting while rendering them with muted, grainy, pencil-like shading and softened outlines, consistent with a pencil-drawn style.
The edited image preserves the original meal and table setting but renders them with muted, desaturated tones and visible fine grain and sketch-like shading consistent with a pencil-drawn style.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive and unstable: several traces call the image complete based on muted tones, grain, and sketch-like shading, while another identifies substantial photographic color/detail and correctly distinguishes progress from a whole-image pencil drawing. In the supplied edit, the scene is visibly desaturated and textured, but retains photographic lighting, smooth forms, and detailed color; that supports progress, not unambiguous completion. Tighten the semantic distinction between pencil-like treatment and the image as a whole reading as a completed pencil drawing, and require the whole-image evidence to assess whether photographic rendering still dominates rather than treating style cues alone as sufficient. Keep s1/s2 as evidence of progress, not proxies for completion; preserve partial when progress is established but s3 explicitly fails, and unresolved when required evidence is unavailable. Do not convert the transport failure in the s3 trace into negative visual evidence or a partial judgment. The reference label is aggregate guidance, not atomic ground truth; use it to investigate the inconsistent completion boundary, not to force a label. Repeated high-confidence variation suggests criterion ambiguity, not absence of the requested edit.
s3: The binding already asks whether the whole image reads as a pencil drawing, but its contrast with “only limited” treatment can make broad desaturation, grain, and softened shading seem sufficient. Clarify the completion boundary in terms of the overall rendering: assess whether forms, lighting, and detail are actually rendered as drawing, or whether photographic rendering still dominates despite pencil-like texture across many objects. In this edit, the muted, grainy treatment is widespread, yet much of the scene retains photographic structure; treat those cues as evidence of progress, not automatic proof of completion. Keep the ancestor’s progress observation separate from this node’s completion judgment, and preserve the rubric’s distinction between partial progress and complete fulfillment. Do not add a monochrome or technique requirement. Treat the transport-failed trace as unavailable evidence, not a visual failure; use repeated high-confidence disagreement to clarify the criterion, not to force the aggregate reference label.
s2: The binding is already scoped to visible, requested changes, but it should make this node’s role explicitly about detecting *any genuine progress*, not deciding whether the whole image is fully transformed. The edit shows broad desaturation, grain, and softened, sketch-like texture across the food and surrounding scene, so those are evidence of progress even though photographic lighting, forms, and detail remain; do not let incomplete fulfillment turn this node’s progress check into a failure. Conversely, avoid treating generic muted color or texture alone as sufficient without image-grounded evidence that it contributes to a pencil-drawing appearance. Keep this node’s finding separate from the downstream completion judgment, so progress can support “partial” when completion is not established. The repeated high-confidence variation points to an ambiguous evidence threshold, not absence of the requested edit. Treat unavailable/transport-failed evidence as unavailable, not as negative visual evidence, and use the aggregate reference only as a diagnostic signal rather than forcing its label.
